why: The first turn whose teacher is not a fixed agent but the loop's own last output, made better (ADR 0055). Three turns have measured that imitation is a fixed point: the better the clone copies, the closer to one half it lands against its own teacher -- 0.5513 to 0.6175 at 96 % copy in ci-118, 0.4875 to 0.4925 at 98.5 % in ci-138. Everything the clone arm improves improves how fast the loop reaches its teacher, never what its teacher is. So this turn changes the teacher instead of the learner: it records `lookahead:policy:models/clone/ci-69/policy.json`, the committed clone with the round played out over it. That operator is measured, not assumed -- against Greedy on the 200 benchmark seeds, both sides, the bare clone scores 0.7250 (0.6775 to 0.7725) in 11.52 rounds with 20 % of matches at the cap, and searched it scores 0.8350 (0.7969 to 0.8731) in 7.61 rounds with 4.5 % and no draws; the intervals do not overlap. The question, and the only one this turn asks: does a clone of that searched play beat the clone it searched with. ci-69 is both the inner agent and the baseline, so `evaluation-vs-baseline.json` is exactly that comparison, and the champion bar plays the new clone against ci-69 head to head for the same reason. An expectation written before the run: the clone should land near its teacher as every clone does, and its teacher is eleven points stronger than ci-69, so it should beat ci-69 measurably. If it does, the loop has climbed for the first time and the next turn searches over the clone this one produces. If it lands at one half against ci-69 despite a strictly stronger teacher, the champion bar is reading a converged arm as a failed one and that is the finding -- the clone arm cannot be judged by what it beats, and the ADR that says so has its measurement. `explore` is off, which drops the second recorded dataset per seed and nothing else: the value policy still fits, on the pure dataset, as it does whenever a turn records no exploring one. That is the point -- the exploring dataset is what the searched teacher would cost twice, and it buys an arm that reads 0.0537 to 0.7550 across three seeds, so dropping it is the one cost saving that does not touch the question the clone arm asks. No clone control either, for the same reason: the terms are not what this turn is about. Budget, measured rather than guessed (ADR 0055 asked for exactly this): recording a match with the searched teacher costs 72 ms here against 37 for search-4, so 1.94 times, and the searched matches are a third shorter so the dataset is smaller, not larger. One recorded dataset per seed instead of two, at 1.94 times each, is 0.97 of what search-4's two cost, and one clone fit instead of two; the 79 minutes search-4's three seeds took is the right ceiling to read this against, well inside the 300-minute limit.
